summary: Encourages researchers to contribute their results to internet standardization and explains how to do so. It describes how academic work has shaped Internet technology, and how the IETF and the Internet Research Task Force can use outside input. It is informational guidance, not a protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: Scientists often invent smart ideas about the internet. This guide is a how-to for taking those ideas to the group that writes the rules, so they can become real.

subtitle: A guide for academic researchers bringing ideas to internet standards

tldr.problem: Academic researchers have valuable ideas but may struggle to navigate the IETF process, which values practical deployability over theoretical perfection and requires consensus-building and community engagement.
tldr.mechanism: This guide explains how to assess whether the IETF is the right venue, how to build community support, how to draft a protocol outline, and how to succeed once work has started by committing time, staying open to collaboration, and prioritizing pragmatism over perfection.
tldr.outcome: Researchers who follow this advice can more efficiently bring their innovations into internet standards; the IETF benefits from external research expertise while avoiding failed standardization efforts.

today: RFC 6417 is an Informational document and has not been obsoleted. It remains the primary guide for researchers seeking to bring their work into internet standardization, and the IETF continues to value external research input.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Internet has roots in academic research, and many of its core improvements come from universities and research labs. When a research idea reaches maturity and needs to be standardized for interoperability, the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) is often the right venue. However, the IETF works differently from academic research: it prioritizes solutions that are both theoretically sound and deployable in today's networks using existing technology, at reasonable cost, and incrementally rather than all at once.

This gap between academic and standards-body culture confuses many researchers. The RFC lists common frustrations: ideas that are too theoretical or high-level, proposals that would require changing too many things at once, lack of clarity about which working group to approach, difficulty giving up control of a proposal, and fatigue from the slow consensus-driven process.
sections.plainLanguage: Scientists think differently than people who run the internet. Scientists want to be right. Internet people want things to actually work right now. This guide helps scientists understand what internet people care about.

sections.title: Deciding Whether the IETF is the Right Venue
sections.content:
Before approaching the IETF, a researcher should answer two fundamental questions: How would the Internet be better if this proposal were standardized and deployed? What Internet nodes (end-hosts, routers, middleboxes, etc.) would need to be upgraded?

The IETF now insists that a proposal solve a current, significant problem, not a theoretical one that might arise in the future. The proposal must be specific about what improvements it brings and in which use cases. It should explain whether both endpoints must adopt it, whether it can fall back to existing protocols, and whether the first or last adopters gain the most benefit.

If the idea is too abstract or high-level, the IRTF (Internet Research Task Force) may be a better fit. If it requires replacing many protocols or upgrading many types of nodes simultaneously, it is probably too ambitious for the IETF, which prefers incremental improvements. Finally, all contributions to the IETF carry intellectual property implications; researchers should be aware of the IETF's "Note Well" policies on patents and publication rights.
sections.plainLanguage: Is this idea about fixing something broken right now, or just a cool idea for later? Will it need to work with old things, or does everything need to change? If it's just a cool idea, maybe a research group is better than the standards group.

sections.title: Getting the IETF to Start Work on Your Proposal
sections.content:
Once a researcher decides the IETF is the right place, three steps help: first, identify the correct working group (WG) or area within the IETF's structure (areas like routing or security contain multiple WGs). Join the relevant mailing list and send an Internet-Draft. If no suitable WG exists, find the right Area and potentially propose a new working group, though this is difficult and usually requires a "Birds of a Feather" (BoF) session at an IETF meeting.

Second, build a community. Standards require agreement and approval from many people. The IETF community needs to see evidence of wider support: comments on the mailing list, co-authored drafts with industry partners or users, and engagement from technical experts who can stress-test the idea. An informal session or bar-BoF at an IETF meeting can help build momentum.

Third, describe your proposal in outline form, not exhaustive detail. Too much detail overwhelms people; outlines make them feel they can contribute. A useful tool is a "protocol model" document that answers three questions: What problem is the protocol solving? What messages are transmitted and what do they mean? What are the important but non-obvious features? Submit as an Internet-Draft, the standard format the IETF community expects.
sections.plainLanguage: Find the right table at the conference. Tell people about your idea on the email list and at meetings. Write it down in a simple way, not every tiny detail, so people think they can help make it better.

sections.title: Increasing the Chances of Successful Standardization
sections.content:
Once the IETF agrees to start work, several practices increase the likelihood of success. First, commit significant time and energy. Even mature proposals typically take a minimum of two years to become standards; face-to-face participation at IETF meetings is important. The IETF works by rough consensus with no top-down process, so perseverance is necessary to prevent decisions from unwinding, but also to recognize when genuine lack of interest means the work should stop.

Second, come with an open mindset. Co-authors should actively develop the proposal, not just lend their names. Once the IETF starts work, it owns the proposal and it is no longer the researcher's alone. Be open to working with others to add security, performance, and operational considerations that the researcher may not have expertise in. When two proposals compete, IETF participants synthesize them rather than treat them as rivals as academics might.

Third, seek a reasonable solution that works, not a perfect one. The research mindset seeks exhaustive investigation; the IETF mindset seeks to solve current problems and iterate later. Over-optimizing may mean the solution becomes obsolete before deployment. Finally, implement the protocol. Running code impresses the IETF and helps discover real issues. Actual implementations increase the chances of real-world deployment.
sections.plainLanguage: Stick with it for years, not weeks. Let others change your idea. Get it good enough, not perfect. Build it and try it out before you expect everyone to use it.

sections.title: Real-World Examples
sections.content:
The RFC includes two examples of successful research-to-standards transitions. Multipath TCP (MPTCP) came from the Trilogy research project and enables a single TCP connection to use multiple paths simultaneously. The team socialized the idea in multiple working groups, created a public mailing list and web page, and held an informal bar-BoF. After verifying traction, they requested a BoF at IETF 75 in Stockholm in July 2009, which was approved. Following community discussion, the MPTCP working group was created in October 2009 and made significant progress on its milestones.

Congestion Exposure (ConEx), also from Trilogy, allows end-hosts to inform the network about congestion they encounter. The team followed a similar path: early socialization at multiple venues, an open mailing list, public materials, and a bar-BoF. A BoF at IETF 76 was initially approved, but the IESG had concerns, so a second BoF was held. The ConEx WG was eventually approved with a narrower scope than originally proposed, illustrating how research aspiration must meet Internet standardization pragmatism. Both examples show the importance of persistence, community building, and willingness to compromise.
sections.plainLanguage: Two research groups took ideas through the whole process. One made TCP use many paths at once; the other lets the network know when things are slow. Both took years and changed along the way as people added ideas and raised concerns.
